title: Better, equal, worse
carry: greed holds on, and conceit measures, even downward

cards: Eleven at night. A shopping cart on a phone holds one thing, then two, then a third that was never on any list. Nothing dramatic has happened.
Nobody was hurt. No rule was broken. And still the mind has been leaning forward for an hour, reaching.
Today the manual introduces one of the families that grows on top of yesterday's four, and the family starts with that lean.

teach.b: The head of the family is lobha, greed. In the Abhidhamma it reaches wider than wanting money. It's any holding on: to a taste, a plan, a person, the feeling of being right.
The Dhammapada puts it in one line, in Max Müller's words: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed."
A torrent carries things away with it. The Abhidhammattha Sangaha gives greed two relatives that appear only in its company.

teach.h: A VIEW CAN BE CLUNG TO.
teach.b: The first is wrong view, ditthi: a view that misreads how things are, held tight. Notice where the manual puts it: with greed, not with anger.
A wrong view, on this account, is something the mind clings to, the way a hand closes around a snack. The second relative is conceit, mana. Conceit is measuring.
The suttas describe it in three shapes: I'm better, I'm equal, I'm worse. All three count. Running yourself down is still measuring, still the self standing on the scale.
And a fine detail: the manual says wrong view and conceit never arise in the same moment. One grips an idea; the other grips a ranking of me.
So the family has three members, wanting, gripping a view, and measuring, and they can look nothing alike: a cart at eleven at night, an argument that has to be won, a quiet comparison at a reunion.
The Abhidhamma's point is that they share one root, the mind leaning toward something and holding on.

how: Abhidhamma students learn greed, wrong view and conceit as the greed-group of unwholesome factors, and some meditation teachers ask students to note 'wanting' or 'comparing' when these arise.

o: greed with its relatives, wrong view and conceit
a household that cares more for money than kindness
the monastic rules on handling money

p: wrong view: a view held tight

s: in the manual, wrong view belongs with greed
a view gripped tight is a kind of holding on.
the suttas name three shapes: better, equal and worse.
wrong view and conceit can arise in the same moment
the manual says they never do: one grips an idea, the other a ranking of me.

games.q: a friend shares good news, and you think, I'll never be as good as her. by the suttas' list, is that conceit?
o: only if it's said out loud.
games.why: the suttas describe conceit in three shapes: I'm better, I'm equal, I'm worse. all three put the self on the scale.

practice: If you'd like, bring to mind someone you saw or heard about recently, a friend, a neighbor, a stranger online, and watch for the scale: does a small voice say better, or worse, or about the same?
That's conceit, the measuring; no need to argue with it, just see the scale come out and let it go back in the drawer. Then return to the breath, which isn't better or worse than anyone's.

wordCard.voice: Greed's family. Greed, wrong view and conceit: wanting, gripping a view, and measuring oneself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali mana: conceit, the mind measuring itself against others.

carryVoice: Your line: greed holds on, and conceit measures, even downward. Wanting, a view held tight, and the scale: one lean. See you tomorrow.
